'''Victoria A. Braithwaite''' (19 July 1967 – 30 September 2019) was an English scientist who was a Professor of Animal Behaviour and Cognition at [[Pennsylvania State University]]. She was the first person to demonstrate that [[Pain in fish|fish feel pain]], which impacted [[animal welfare]] research and changed guidelines for the treatment of fish in laboratories and fisheries in the UK, Europe, and Canada.

== Early life and education ==

Braithwaite was born in [[Bradford]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2019/oct/24/victoria-braithwaite-obituary|title=Victoria Braithwaite obituary|last=Healy|first=Susan|date=24 October 2019|work=The Guardian|access-date=31 October 2019|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref> She was one of seven children.<ref name=":0" /> Her mother, June Pickles, was chair of the Halifax magistrates' bench, and her father, Alan Braithwaite, was a company director. She attended [[Bradford Grammar School]], where she was not encouraged to apply to the [[University of Oxford]].<ref name=":0" /> She did not take this advice, and eventually completed her undergraduate degree in zoology and doctoral degree, supported by a Christopher Welch scholarship, at the [[Somerville College, Oxford]]. Her thesis considered the visual information used by [[Homing pigeon|homing pigeons]] to return to their nests.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.the-scientist.com/news-opinion/fish-biologist-victoria-braithwaite-dies-66650|title=Fish Biologist Victoria Braithwaite Dies|website=The Scientist Magazine|language=en|access-date=31 October 2019|archive-date=18 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200718193516/https://www.the-scientist.com/news-opinion/fish-biologist-victoria-braithwaite-dies-66650|url-status=dead}}</ref> She demonstrated that birds fly home faster when they see their surroundings before being released.<ref name=":0" /> She joined the [[University of Glasgow]] where she studied the cognitive abilities of [[salmon]]. It was during this project that she became interested in animal behaviour.<ref name=":0" />

== Research and career ==
Braithwaite spent her career investigating the cognitive abilities of fish and other animals.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.psu.edu/dept/braithwaite/victoria.html|title=Victoria - Victoria Braithwaite|website=psu.edu|access-date=31 October 2019}}</ref> She showed that fish which live in stable environments (like ponds) use visual markers for guides, whereas fish that live in rivers learn directions using sequences (like left, right, left, right). Her research was the first to show that an animal's cognition is shaped by the worlds in which they live. To recognise her contributions to our understanding of animal navigation, Braithwaite was elected to the [[Royal Institute of Navigation]] in 2005. 

She moved to the [[University of Edinburgh]] in 1995 where she began to investigate whether or not fish felt pain &ndash; so-called [[nociception]].<ref name=":1" /> Whilst it was well understood that chickens and sheep experienced pain, before Braithwaite it was not known whether or not fish did too.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hcn.org/issues/51.6/fish-how-should-we-treat-fish-before-they-end-up-on-our-plates|title=How should we treat fish before they end up on our plates?|date=20 March 2019|author=Ben Goldfarb|website=hcn.org|language=en-us|access-date=31 October 2019}}</ref> She demonstrated fish felt pain using a series of experiments, the first of which included showing that fish contained the correct anatomy to detect pain ([[Nociceptor|nociceptors]]).<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/fish-feel-pain-180967764/|title=It's Official: Fish Feel Pain|website=Smithsonian|language=en|access-date=31 October 2019}}</ref> She showed that fish produce pain-killing [[opioids]] in the same way that mammals do.<ref name=":2" /> She then investigated whether or not they responded to stimuli, and demonstrated that these receptors feel bodily damage and that fish behaviour is different when they are exposed to an unpleasant stimulus. She then demonstrated that fish that had been exposed to an unpleasant stimulus, for example, vinegar, behaved differently when made to perform tasks after they had taken human painkillers.<ref name=":0" /> Her work changed protocols regulating the ways fish are treated in laboratories and fisheries in the UK, Europe, and Canada.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hcn.org/articles/fish-how-should-we-treat-fish-before-they-end-up-on-our-plates|title=The Right Way to Kill a Fish|last=Goldfarb|first=Ben |work=High Country News|date=26 March 2019|access-date=31 October 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.psu.edu/story/141957/2012/05/17/research/touch-withvictoria-braithwaite|title=In Touch With...Victoria Braithwaite |website=news.psu.edu|access-date=31 October 2019}}</ref> As of 2019 other countries were also considering making such changes.<ref name=":0" />

Braithwaite joined [[Pennsylvania State University]] in 2007, where she was appointed Professor of Fisheries and Biology.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Here she demonstrated that providing a more natural environment for fish impacted their cognitive abilities and likelihood to survive in the world.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.psu.edu/story/590550/2019/09/30/research/penn-state-community-grieves-loss-biologist-victoria-braithwaite|title=Penn State community grieves loss of biologist Victoria Braithwaite |website=news.psu.edu|language=en|access-date=31 October 2019}}</ref> Before Braithwaite's work, fish that had been reared in tanks did not survive when they were released into the world.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.psu.edu/story/283065/2013/07/31/research/aquatic-playground-can-turn-water-tanks-fish-schools|title=Aquatic playground can turn water tanks into fish schools |website=news.psu.edu|language=en|access-date=31 October 2019}}</ref> Whilst a visiting fellow at the [[Berlin Institute for Advanced Study]] in 2015, Braithwaite analysed the inferences that could be made about animal pain and other emotional states. She was offered the directorship of the IGB Leibniz-Institute of Freshwater Ecology and Inland Fisheries in 2018,<ref name=":0" /> but was unable to assume the position.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.igb-berlin.de/en/news/we-grieve-loss-victoria-braithwaite|title=We grieve the Loss of Victoria Braithwaite|website=www.igb-berlin.de|date=October 2019 |access-date=1 December 2019}}</ref>

== Awards and honours ==
* 2005 Fellow of the [[Royal Institute of Navigation]]<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://humaneheartland.org/scientific-advisory-committee/item/victoria-braithwaite|title=Victoria Braithwaite, PhD|website=humaneheartland.org|access-date=31 October 2019}}</ref>
* 2006 [[Fisheries Society of the British Isles]] [[FSBI Medal|Medal]]<ref name=":3" />
* 2016 Fellow of the [[Linnean Society of London]]<ref name=":3" />

== Personal life ==
Braithwaite in 1992 married the evolutionary biologist [[Andrew F. Read|Andrew Read]]; they eventually divorced.<ref name=":0" /> Together they had two sons.<ref name=":0" /> In 2018 she was diagnosed with [[pancreatic cancer]].<ref name=":1" /> She died on 30 September 2019.<ref name=":0"/>
